headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% in September as fuel costs surge, raising hopes of a Bank of England rate rise

terms.meaning: The Consumer Prices Index, the main measure of how fast prices are rising.
Inflation with the most volatile items, such as energy and food, left out.
A country that buys in more energy than it produces.

levels.headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% in September as fuel costs surge, raising hopes of a Bank of England rate rise
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% expected in a Reuters poll, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.
Transport made the largest upward contribution, with transport inflation rising to 6.6% from 4.6%. Motor fuel prices were 29.8% higher than a year earlier. Britain is a net energy importer, which leaves it exposed to external shocks such as the US-Iran war and the struggle to move oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
Core inflation, which strips out volatile items, rose to 2.8%, its highest since March, while services inflation accelerated to 3.7%.
The Bank of England's Bank Rate is 3.75%, against an inflation target of 2%. Markets widely expect the Bank to raise rates at its meeting on 5 November. The next inflation figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: It shows energy costs are feeding through to the wider economy, which raises the chance that borrowing costs go up.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% as energy shock feeds through to transport and services
levels.body:
Annual consumer price inflation reached 3.5% in September, from 3.1% in August, the ONS reported, beating the 3.4% forecast in a Reuters poll.
The biggest upward push came from transport, where inflation climbed to 6.6% from 4.6%, and motor fuel prices were up 29.8% on a year earlier. Because Britain is a net energy importer, it is vulnerable to the US-Iran war and the disruption to oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz.
The underlying picture also worsened. Core inflation, which excludes volatile elements, rose to 2.8%, the highest since March, and services inflation, closely watched by the Bank of England, accelerated to 3.7%.
With Bank Rate at 3.75% and the target at 2%, traders expect a rise at the Bank's 5 November meeting. The next release is on 18 November.
levels.why: Sticky services inflation is what central bankers watch most, so this reading strengthens the case for higher rates.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% as fuel prices climb, with an interest rate rise expected
levels.body:
UK inflation rose to 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August, according to the ONS. Economists had expected 3.4%.
The main driver was transport. Prices in that category rose 6.6% over the year, compared with 4.6% the month before, and petrol and diesel were 29.8% dearer than a year ago. Britain imports a lot of its energy, so it feels the effect of the war involving the US and Iran and the problems moving oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
Core inflation, which leaves out items such as energy, rose to 2.8%, its highest since March. Services inflation reached 3.7%.
The Bank of England wants inflation at 2% and currently holds its main rate at 3.75%. It is widely expected to raise it at its next meeting on 5 November.
levels.why: Higher prices squeeze household budgets, and a higher interest rate would make mortgages and loans more expensive.

levels.headline: UK inflation climbs to 3.5% as petrol and diesel prices bite
levels.body:
UK inflation rose to 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August, official figures show. Economists had predicted 3.4%, so the number was a surprise on the upside.
Fuel was the main cause. Petrol and diesel cost 29.8% more than a year ago, and transport prices overall rose 6.6% over the year. Britain imports much of its energy, so it is exposed to the war involving the US and Iran and to disruption to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
A measure called core inflation, which leaves out volatile items such as energy, rose to 2.8%, its highest since March. Services inflation reached 3.7%.
The Bank of England aims for 2% and is widely expected to raise interest rates from 3.75% on 5 November. The next figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: Rising prices cut what wages buy, and a rate rise would make mortgages and loans dearer.

levels.headline: UK prices rose 3.5% in the year to September, mostly because of fuel
levels.body:
Inflation, the rate at which prices rise, reached 3.5% in the UK in the 12 months to September. In August it was 3.1%. The Office for National Statistics published the figure, and it was a little higher than the 3.4% experts had predicted.
Fuel was the main reason. Petrol and diesel cost 29.8% more than a year earlier. Britain buys a lot of its energy from other countries, so it is hit when oil gets expensive. Oil prices have jumped because of the war between the US and Iran and trouble moving ships through the Strait of Hormuz, a key sea route for oil.
A measure called core inflation, which leaves out items whose prices jump around, rose to 2.8%.
The Bank of England aims for 2%. It is expected to raise interest rates on 5 November.
levels.why: Your money buys less than it did, and loans and mortgages could soon cost more.

levels.headline: Prices in the UK are rising faster, with petrol and diesel the biggest cause
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year before. The month before, the figure was 3.1%. This yearly rise in prices is called inflation. The Office for National Statistics reported it, and it was slightly more than experts guessed.
Petrol and diesel were the biggest reason, costing nearly 30% more than last year. The UK buys in a lot of its energy, so when the price of oil goes up because of a war in the Middle East, we feel it at the pumps. Shipping oil through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz has been difficult.
The Bank of England wants prices to rise by only 2% a year. Its main interest rate is 3.75%, and it is expected to raise it on 5 November to slow price rises.
levels.why: Everyday costs are climbing, and borrowing money could get dearer soon.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster in the UK because fuel costs so much more
levels.body:
Prices in the UK went up by 3.5% over the last year. A month earlier, they had gone up by 3.1%. When prices keep rising like this, it is called inflation. It means the same money buys a bit less than before.
The biggest reason is the cost of petrol and diesel, which is almost 30% higher than last year. The UK buys a lot of its fuel from other countries. There is a war involving the US and Iran, and ships are finding it hard to carry oil through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. That pushes up the price of oil.
The Bank of England wants prices to rise by about 2% a year. It sets the main interest rate, which is 3.75% now. People expect it to raise that rate on 5 November.
levels.why: Shopping, travel and heating can cost more, and loans may become dearer.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster, mainly because petrol and diesel cost more
levels.body:
Over the past year, prices in the UK went up by 3.5%. Last month the figure was 3.1%. A rise in prices like this is called inflation. It means that what you can buy with your pocket money or wages gets smaller.
The main reason is fuel. Petrol and diesel now cost nearly 30% more than a year ago. The UK buys a lot of its fuel from other countries. A war involving the US and Iran has made oil more expensive, and it is hard to move oil by ship through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz.
The Bank of England is the bank that looks after the country's money. It wants prices to rise by only 2% a year. It sets an interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. Many people think it will raise that rate on 5 November.
levels.why: Things in shops cost more, and borrowing money may get more expensive.

levels.headline: Things cost more than they did last year, and fuel is the main reason
levels.body:
Prices in the UK are now 3.5% higher than a year ago. A month ago they were 3.1% higher. When prices rise like this, we call it inflation. It means a pound buys a little less than it used to.
Petrol and diesel cost much more now. They are nearly 30% dearer than last year. The UK buys a lot of its fuel from other countries. There is a war in the Middle East, and it has made oil costly. Ships also find it hard to sail through one narrow stretch of sea that oil travels along.
The Bank of England is a special bank for the whole country. It wants prices to go up slowly, by about 2% a year. It can change the interest rate, which is the extra money you pay when you borrow. It may raise it on 5 November.
levels.why: Your money may stretch less far, and loans may cost more.

levels.headline: Why things in the shop cost a bit more than last year
levels.body:
Imagine a sweet that cost one pound last year. Now it costs a few pence more. When lots of things cost a bit more, grown-ups call it inflation. In the UK, prices have gone up by about three and a half pounds in every hundred pounds over the last year.
The biggest reason is petrol and diesel. Cars, buses and lorries need them. They cost nearly a third more than last year. A war far away has made oil dear, and it is hard to move oil on ships.
There is a big bank for the whole country called the Bank of England. It wants prices to rise only a tiny bit. It might make borrowing money cost more, a bit like charging extra for lending a toy. That is called raising the interest rate. Grown-ups think it may happen on 5 November.
levels.why: Families may find that their money buys a little less than before.

headline: Wall Street closes higher on Monday as the S&P 500 gains 0.70% to 7,676.77 on Anthropic IPO excitement

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 of the largest US companies.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, an index of 30 big US companies.
An index dominated by technology companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange.

levels.headline: Wall Street closes higher on Monday as the S&P 500 gains 0.70% to 7,676.77 on Anthropic IPO excitement
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed up on Monday 26 October, the last completed session, rising 0.70% to 7,676.77, according to CNBC. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained about 0.28% to finish at 52,361.58, and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.82% to 26,169.38. Trading Economics showed a marginally different S&P 500 close of 7,678.38, so figures vary slightly by source.
Technology led the gains. CNBC said the artificial intelligence trade was lifted after Anthropic filed to go public on the Nasdaq, and chip stocks were among the strongest performers. The rebound followed a weak stretch for AI-related shares, with the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq coming off back-to-back weekly losses.
Investors now look ahead to the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision on Wednesday 28 October.
levels.why: Wall Street moves affect pension funds and savings around the world, and the Fed decision could move markets again.

levels.headline: US stocks rebound on Monday, with tech and chip shares leading the S&P 500 up 0.70%
levels.body:
US stocks closed higher on Monday 26 October. The S&P 500 rose 0.70% to 7,676.77 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.82% to 26,169.38, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average added about 0.28% to 52,361.58, CNBC reported. Another data provider put the S&P 500 close slightly higher, at 7,678.38.
The move was driven mainly by technology. Anthropic's filing to list on the Nasdaq gave the artificial intelligence trade a lift, and semiconductor shares led the advance after a weak patch for AI-linked names.
The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq had both ended the previous two weeks lower. Attention now turns to the Federal Reserve, whose rate decision is due on Wednesday.
levels.why: A rebound after two weak weeks shows how much US markets depend on confidence in artificial intelligence.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends Monday higher as tech stocks rally after the Anthropic IPO filing
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed higher on Monday 26 October, the latest completed trading day. It rose 0.70% to 7,676.77, according to CNBC. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained about 0.28% to 52,361.58, and the technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose 0.82% to 26,169.38.
Technology companies led the way. CNBC said the news that Anthropic had filed to float on the Nasdaq boosted enthusiasm for artificial intelligence shares, with companies that make computer chips doing especially well. This followed a poor stretch, as both the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq had lost ground in each of the last two weeks.
Investors are now waiting for the Federal Reserve's decision on interest rates on Wednesday.
levels.why: Share prices influence pensions and savings, and shifts in tech stocks can spread to markets elsewhere.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends Monday higher, led by technology shares
levels.body:
US shares rose on Monday 26 October, the last completed session. The S&P 500 gained 0.70% to close at 7,676.77, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose about 0.28% to 52,361.58, and the Nasdaq Composite climbed 0.82% to 26,169.38, according to CNBC.

levels.headline: US shares rise on Monday, led by technology companies

US share prices went up on Monday 26 October, the last full day of trading. The S&P 500, an index of 500 big US companies, rose 0.70% to 7,676.77. The Dow, which follows 30 large firms, rose about 0.28% to 52,361.58. The Nasdaq, packed with tech companies, rose 0.82% to 26,169.38.

levels.headline: US stock markets finished higher on Monday

levels.headline: American share prices went up on Monday, mostly for technology companies

On Monday 26 October, share prices in the United States went up. Shares are tiny pieces of companies. People buy them hoping they will be worth more later. levels.headline: Share prices went up in America on Monday
levels.body:
Think of a market where people buy and sell tiny pieces of companies. Those pieces are called shares. On Monday, in America, the prices of lots of shares went up. That was good news for people who own them. It is like finding that your collection of football cards is now worth a little more than yesterday.
The biggest rises were in technology companies. These are firms that make computers, chips and clever programs. One company called Anthropic, which makes artificial intelligence, said it wants to sell its own shares to the public. That got people excited.
The week before had been a poor one for shares, so Monday felt like a bounce back. On Wednesday, the big bank for the whole of America will decide about interest rates. Everyone is waiting to hear.

headline: Markets price a near-certain Bank of England rate rise to 4% on 5 November

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences the cost of mortgages and loans.
One hundredth of a percentage point, so 25 basis points is 0.25%.
The Monetary Policy Committee, the group that sets interest rates at the Bank of England.

levels.headline: Markets price a near-certain Bank of England rate rise to 4% on 5 November
levels.body:
Financial markets are pricing a 98% chance that the Bank of England will raise Bank Rate by 25 basis points, from 3.75% to 4%, at its next meeting on 5 November, following a stronger-than-expected inflation reading. It would be the first increase since 2023.
In September, the Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 to hold rates at 3.75%, with the three dissenters preferring a rise to 4%. Since then, September inflation has come in at 3.5%, above the 3.4% forecast, with core inflation at 2.8% and services inflation at 3.7%.
Most traders also expect a further rise in December. The Bank's inflation target is 2%, and the Treasury's October compilation of independent forecasts puts inflation in the final quarter of 2026 at around 3.6%.
The next inflation figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: Interest rate decisions shape what households pay on mortgages and loans, and what savers earn.

levels.headline: Traders see a Bank of England hike to 4% next week as inflation surprises on the upside
levels.body:
Markets are pricing a 98% probability that the Bank of England raises Bank Rate by 25 basis points to 4% on 5 November, after September inflation of 3.5% beat expectations. It would be the first rise since 2023.
The Monetary Policy Committee held rates at 3.75% in September by six votes to three, with the minority wanting 4%. The latest data, including core inflation at 2.8% and services inflation at 3.7%, strengthens their case.
Most traders also expect another increase in December. Against an inflation target of 2%, a Treasury compilation of independent forecasts published this month points to inflation of around 3.6% in the fourth quarter of 2026.
The Bank's decision follows a run of price pressures linked to energy costs. The next inflation release is on 18 November.
levels.why: A second rise in December is also expected, so borrowing costs could keep climbing.

levels.headline: A Bank of England interest rate rise to 4% is expected on 5 November
levels.body:
Financial markets now see a 98% chance that the Bank of England will raise its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4% on 5 November. That would be the first rise since 2023. The expectation grew after UK inflation came in at 3.5% for September, higher than forecast.
In September the Bank's rate-setting committee voted 6-3 to keep the rate at 3.75%. The three who lost the vote wanted an increase to 4%. Most traders also expect a further rise in December.
The Bank's target is for inflation to be 2%, so it uses higher interest rates to cool spending and slow price rises. A group of independent forecasts compiled by the Treasury in October suggests inflation will be around 3.6% at the end of this year.
The next inflation figures arrive on 18 November.
levels.why: Mortgage holders and borrowers could pay more, while savers might see better rates.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to raise interest rates to 4% next week
levels.body:
Financial markets are almost certain that the Bank of England will raise its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4% on 5 November. Traders put the chance at 98%. It would be the first increase since 2023.
The move is expected after UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September, above forecasts. The Bank wants inflation to be 2%, and raising rates is its usual tool for slowing price rises, because dearer borrowing tends to reduce spending.
In September, the committee that sets the rate voted 6-3 to hold it. The three who disagreed wanted 4%. Most traders also expect another rise in December.
The next inflation figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: Mortgages and loans could get dearer, though savings rates may improve.

levels.headline: Markets expect the Bank of England to raise interest rates to 4%
levels.body:
People who trade in financial markets think it is almost certain that the Bank of England will raise its main interest rate on 5 November. They put the chance at 98%. The rate would go from 3.75% to 4%. It would be the first rise since 2023.
The reason is inflation, which means prices rising. In September it reached 3.5%, which was higher than experts had guessed. The Bank wants it to be 2%. Raising interest rates makes borrowing more expensive, which can slow spending and help bring prices under control.
In September, the nine people who set the rate voted 6-3 to leave it alone. Three wanted a rise to 4%. Most traders now expect another rise in December as well.
New inflation figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: A higher rate means dearer mortgages and loans, though savers may earn a little more.

levels.headline: The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates next week
levels.body:
Many people who work in financial markets think the Bank of England will make its main interest rate higher on 5 November. They say there is a 98% chance. The rate would rise from 3.75% to 4%. The last time it went up was in 2023.
The Bank does this when prices are rising too fast. In September, prices were 3.5% higher than a year before. The Bank wants the figure to be about 2%. A higher interest rate makes borrowing money cost more. People then tend to spend less, which helps slow down price rises.
Last time, in September, a group of nine people at the Bank voted. Six wanted to leave the rate alone. Three wanted it higher. Most traders also think there will be another rise in December.
levels.why: If rates go up, mortgages and loans cost more, while savings may earn a bit more.

levels.headline: People expect the Bank of England to put interest rates up on 5 November
levels.body:
Almost everyone who buys and sells in the money markets thinks the Bank of England will raise its main interest rate on 5 November. They say there is a 98% chance. The rate would go up from 3.75% to 4%. The last time the Bank did this was in 2023.
Why? Because prices are going up too fast. In September, prices were 3.5% higher than a year earlier. The Bank wants them to rise by about 2%. A higher interest rate makes it cost more to borrow. When borrowing costs more, people spend less. That helps slow price rises.
In September, nine people at the Bank voted on the rate. Six voted to keep it the same, and three voted to raise it. Most traders now expect another rise in December too.
levels.why: Loans and mortgages could cost more, and savings accounts might pay a little more.

levels.headline: The Bank of England will probably make borrowing cost more
levels.body:
The Bank of England looks after the country's money. One of its jobs is to set the interest rate. This is the extra you pay when you borrow money, and the extra you get when you save it. Right now it is 3.75%. People who watch money closely think the Bank will raise it to 4% on 5 November. They think it is almost certain.
The Bank does this because prices are going up too fast. In September, prices were 3.5% higher than last year. The Bank wants only about 2%. When borrowing costs more, people spend less, and prices rise more slowly.
It has not raised the rate since 2023. Many people also think it will raise it again in December.
levels.why: Families with loans or mortgages could pay more, and savers might earn a bit more.

levels.headline: The country's bank is likely to raise the price of borrowing money
levels.body:
Banks charge extra when you borrow money. That extra is called interest. The Bank of England is a special bank for the whole country, and it decides a main interest rate that other banks follow. Right now the rate is 3.75 out of every 100 pounds. Most experts think the Bank will make it 4 out of every 100 pounds on 5 November.
Why would it do that? Prices in shops are going up too fast. They rose by 3.5% over the last year, and the Bank wants them to rise by only about 2%. If borrowing costs more, people spend less, and prices stop rising so quickly.
The Bank has not done this since 2023. People think it may even do it again in December.
levels.why: Grown-ups with loans may have to pay more, but those who save may earn more.

levels.headline: A big bank may charge more to lend money
levels.body:
Imagine you lend your friend some pocket money. You might ask for a tiny bit extra back as a thank you. That extra is called interest. Banks do this too. There is a very important bank for the whole country, called the Bank of England. It decides how much extra banks should ask for.
Right now, the extra is a little under four pounds for every hundred pounds. Experts think the Bank will make it a little more, on 5 November. They are nearly sure.
Why? Because things in shops cost more than last year. If borrowing costs more, people buy less, and prices stop going up so fast. The Bank has not done this for a few years. Experts think it might do it again in December.
levels.why: It can change how much grown-ups pay back on loans, and how much they earn on savings.

headline: Chancellor to deliver the Budget on Wednesday 28 October with inflation and borrowing costs in focus

terms.meaning: The Chancellor's yearly statement of the government's tax and spending plans.
The gap between expected borrowing and the limit the Chancellor has set  under the fiscal rules.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent body that forecasts the economy and public finances.

levels.headline: Chancellor to deliver the Budget on Wednesday 28 October with inflation and borrowing costs in focus
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, will present the Budget on Wednesday 28 October, a date the government announced on 31 July. Government said it would be a Budget to move power and money out of Westminster and into every postcode around Britain, and one built on fiscal discipline.
It arrives with the economy under pressure. Inflation rose to 3.5% in September, and the Bank of England is widely expected to raise Bank Rate from 3.75% on 5 November.
The Budget is also the main test of the government's fiscal rules, since the Office for Budget Responsibility now gives its formal assessment of them only in the autumn. At the Spring Statement in March the government said it had £23.6 billion of headroom against its main borrowing target for 2029-30.
Confirmed details of the tax and spending measures were not available, so none are reported here.
levels.why: The Budget sets the tax and spending plans that affect households, businesses and public services.

levels.headline: Budget day arrives on Wednesday as the Chancellor faces rising prices and a likely interest rate rise
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will deliver the Budget on Wednesday 28 October. The government set the date on 31 July and promised a Budget that moves power and money out of Westminster and into every postcode in Britain, while staying disciplined with the public finances.
The backdrop is difficult. UK inflation climbed to 3.5% in September and markets expect the Bank of England to lift Bank Rate from 3.75% on 5 November, which would raise the government's own borrowing costs over time.
The OBR now publishes its verdict on the fiscal rules only in the autumn, so this Budget is the key test. In March the government reported £23.6 billion of headroom against its main borrowing target for 2029-30.
Specific tax and spending measures have not been confirmed in the sources reviewed.
levels.why: Higher borrowing costs can shrink the room the Chancellor has to cut taxes or raise spending.

levels.headline: The Budget is due on Wednesday, with rising prices and borrowing costs in the background
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will give the Budget on Wednesday 28 October. The government announced the date on 31 July and said the Budget would move power and money away from Westminster to places across Britain, with careful control of public money.
Prices are rising faster. Inflation reached 3.5% in September, and the Bank of England is expected to raise its main interest rate from 3.75% on 5 November. A higher rate can also make it dearer for the government to borrow.
The independent Office for Budget Responsibility will now check whether the government meets its own borrowing rules. In March the government said it had £23.6 billion of room against its main borrowing target for 2029-30.
The exact tax and spending changes have not been confirmed, so they are not covered here.
levels.why: The Budget decides how much tax people pay and how much money goes to schools, hospitals and councils.

levels.headline: Chancellor to present the Budget on Wednesday amid rising prices
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, will present the Budget on Wednesday 28 October. The date was announced on 31 July, and the government has described it as a Budget to move power and money out of Westminster and into every postcode around Britain, built on fiscal discipline.
It comes as inflation has risen to 3.5% and the Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates from 3.75% on 5 November. Higher rates can make it dearer for the government to borrow.
The independent Office for Budget Responsibility now gives its judgement on the government's borrowing rules only in the autumn. At the Spring Statement in March, the government said it had £23.6 billion of headroom against its main target for 2029-30.
The specific measures have not been confirmed.
levels.why: The Budget affects taxes, public services and the room the government has to spend.

levels.headline: The Chancellor will set out the government's tax and spending plans on Wednesday
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, will give the Budget on Wednesday 28 October. A Budget is a yearly speech in which the Chancellor explains how much the government plans to spend, and how it will raise the money through taxes. The government has said this one will move money and power out of London and into every part of Britain.
Prices are rising quickly, with inflation at 3.5%. The Bank of England is also expected to raise interest rates on 5 November. That makes borrowing more costly for everyone, including the government.
The government has rules about how much it can borrow. An independent group, the Office for Budget Responsibility, checks whether it is keeping to them.
The details of the plans have not been confirmed yet.
levels.why: The Budget affects taxes, public services and how much room the government has to spend.

levels.headline: The Budget is on Wednesday: the Chancellor will say how the government plans to spend and tax
levels.body:
On Wednesday 28 October, the Chancellor, John Healey, will give a speech called the Budget. In it, the Chancellor explains how much money the government will spend and how much it will take in through taxes, such as income tax. The government says it wants to share money and power with more parts of the country, not just London, and to be careful with money.
This comes at a hard time. Prices are going up faster, at 3.5% a year, and the Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates soon. That makes borrowing dearer, even for the government.
The government has rules to stop it borrowing too much. A watchdog called the OBR checks that it keeps to them.
We do not yet know what the Budget will contain.
levels.why: It can change how much tax you pay and how much the government can spend on public services.

levels.headline: The Chancellor gives his big money speech on Wednesday
levels.body:
On Wednesday 28 October, the Chancellor will give a big speech called the Budget. The Chancellor is the minister in charge of the country's money, and the current Chancellor is John Healey. In the speech, the Chancellor tells us how much the government plans to spend and how much it will collect in taxes. Taxes are money that people and firms pay to the government to run schools, hospitals and roads.
The government says it wants to give more money and power to places all over Britain, not only London.
Prices are going up quickly at the moment, and interest rates may go up too. That makes borrowing dearer for families and for the government.
We do not know yet what will be in the Budget.
levels.why: The Budget helps decide the taxes we pay and the services we get.

levels.headline: A big speech about the country's money happens on Wednesday
levels.body:
Every year, the person in charge of the country's money gives a big speech. This is called the Budget. This year it is on Wednesday 28 October. The person is the Chancellor, and the current Chancellor is John Healey. The Chancellor will say how much money the government will spend and how much it will collect in taxes. Taxes are money people pay so the government can run schools, hospitals and roads.
The government has said it wants to spread money and power to every part of Britain. Prices are going up quite fast right now, so people are watching closely. The Bank of England may also make borrowing cost more soon.
Nobody outside the government knows yet what the speech will say.
levels.why: It decides some of the taxes grown-ups pay and how much money goes to public services.

levels.headline: The country's money speech is on Wednesday
levels.body:
The government has a pot of money. It collects it from taxes. Taxes are the money that people and firms give to the government. The government spends it on things we all share, like schools, hospitals and roads. Once a year, the Chancellor, who looks after the pot, makes a speech called the Budget to explain the plan. This year the Chancellor is John Healey, and the speech is on Wednesday 28 October.
The government says it wants to share money and power with every part of Britain.
Things in shops cost more than before, so it is a tricky time to plan. Nobody yet knows what the plan will be.
levels.why: It helps decide how much grown-ups pay in tax and what the government can afford to do.

levels.headline: A grown-up in charge of the country's money explains the plan on Wednesday
levels.body:
Imagine your class has a big jar of money that everyone puts a little into. The teacher uses it to buy paper, pens and books for everyone. Once a year, the teacher explains the plan for the jar. For our country, the jar is full of money from taxes, and the grown-up in charge is called the Chancellor. The Chancellor is John Healey.
His plan is called the Budget. He will say it on Wednesday 28 October. The government says it wants to share money and power with every part of Britain, not just one big city.
Prices have been going up, so it is a tricky time. We will find out the plan on Wednesday.
levels.why: The plan decides how much grown-ups give to the shared jar, and what it is spent on.

headline: UK unemployment falls to 4.7% but ONS describes the labour market as broadly flat

terms.meaning: The share of people who want a job and are looking for one, but do not have one.
Being out of work and not looking for a job, for example because of study, illness or caring.
People recorded as being paid by an employer through the tax system.

levels.headline: UK unemployment falls to 4.7% but ONS describes the labour market as broadly flat
levels.body:
The UK unemployment rate was 4.7% in the three months to August, down 0.1 percentage points on both the previous quarter and the year before, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on 20 October. About 1.71 million people were unemployed. The rate was 5.1% for men and 4.3% for women.
The employment rate for 16 to 64 year olds was 75.3%, and about 9.09 million people in that age range were economically inactive.
The ONS described the labour market as broadly flat in 2026. The number of payrolled employees has fallen, and vacancies recorded their largest fall of the year, mainly among smaller firms that cite higher labour costs. Regular pay growth has been fairly steady, though the ONS noted weakness in total pay.
The next labour market figures are due on 17 November.
levels.why: Jobs and wages shape household incomes, and they influence whether the Bank of England raises interest rates.

levels.headline: UK unemployment dips to 4.7% as vacancies fall, with the ONS calling the job market flat
levels.body:
The unemployment rate stood at 4.7% for June to August 2026, a fall of 0.1 percentage points on both the latest quarter and the year, according to the ONS figures published on 20 October. That is about 1.71 million people, with a rate of 5.1% for men and 4.3% for women.
The employment rate among 16 to 64 year olds was 75.3%, while around 9.09 million people in that age group were economically inactive.
Beneath the headline, the picture is subdued. The ONS characterised the labour market as broadly flat this year, with fewer payrolled employees and the biggest drop in vacancies of 2026, concentrated in smaller firms that point to higher labour costs. Regular pay growth is fairly steady but total pay is weaker.
The next release is on 17 November.
levels.why: A flat job market with falling vacancies can make it harder for people to move jobs or find work.

levels.headline: UK unemployment falls slightly to 4.7%, but job vacancies drop
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics reported on 20 October that unemployment in the UK was 4.7% between June and August 2026. That is 0.1 percentage points lower than three months earlier and a year earlier. Around 1.71 million people were unemployed.
The employment rate for people aged 16 to 64 was 75.3%. About 9.09 million people in that age group were economically inactive, which means they were neither working nor looking for work.
The ONS said the job market has been broadly flat in 2026. The number of employees on company payrolls has fallen, and vacancies had their biggest fall of the year. Many smaller firms said higher costs of employing people were holding them back. Regular pay growth has been fairly steady.
New figures are due on 17 November.
levels.why: Fewer vacancies and weaker pay mean less security for workers, even if unemployment dips.

levels.headline: UK unemployment dips to 4.7% as the jobs market stays flat
levels.body:
UK unemployment was 4.7% in the three months to August, down slightly on both the previous quarter and a year ago, the Office for National Statistics said on 20 October. About 1.71 million people were out of work, and looking for a job.
The employment rate for people aged 16 to 64 was 75.3%. About 9.09 million people in that age group were neither working nor looking for work, which is known as economic inactivity.
The ONS described the jobs market as broadly flat this year. The number of employees on company payrolls has fallen, and job vacancies saw their biggest fall of the year, mostly at smaller firms that point to higher costs of employing people. Regular pay growth has been fairly steady.
The next figures are due on 17 November.
levels.why: Fewer vacancies make it harder for people to change jobs or ask for a pay rise.

levels.headline: UK unemployment is 4.7%, a small fall, but there are fewer job vacancies
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics said that 4.7% of people who wanted a job in the UK did not have one between June and August. That is slightly down from 4.8% both three months earlier and a year earlier. About 1.71 million people were without work. The ONS published this on 20 October.
About three in four people aged 16 to 64 had a job. Another 9.09 million people in that age group were not working and were not looking for work, which is called economic inactivity. People can be inactive because they are studying, ill or caring for someone.
The ONS said the job market has been mostly flat this year. Fewer people are on company payrolls, and the number of job vacancies fell by the most this year. Smaller firms say higher costs are the reason.
levels.why: Fewer vacancies make it harder for people to find new jobs or ask for pay rises.

levels.headline: Fewer people are out of work in the UK, but there are fewer new jobs on offer
levels.body:
Between June and August, 4.7 in every 100 people who wanted a job in the UK could not find one. That figure is a little lower than it was three months ago and a year ago. About 1.71 million people were looking for work. The Office for National Statistics reported this on 20 October.
About 75 in every 100 people aged 16 to 64 had a job. Another 9.09 million people in that age group were not working and not looking for work. They may be studying, ill or looking after family.
The ONS described the job market as flat. Fewer people are on company payrolls, and fewer job vacancies are being advertised. Small firms say that employing people costs them more than it used to.
levels.why: It is harder to find a new job when fewer jobs are advertised.

levels.headline: Slightly fewer people are looking for work, but there are fewer jobs being advertised
levels.body:
Between June and August, about 5 in every 100 people in the UK who wanted a job could not find one. The exact number is 4.7%. That is a little lower than a few months ago and a year ago. About 1.7 million people were looking for work. The Office for National Statistics, which counts these things for the government, shared the news on 20 October.
About three out of four adults of working age had jobs. Millions of others were not looking for work. They might be studying, unwell or looking after someone.
The ONS said the job market is not moving much. Fewer people are being paid by companies than before, and fewer jobs are being advertised. Small firms say that paying workers now costs them more.
levels.why: If fewer jobs are advertised, it can be hard to find work or move to a better job.

levels.headline: A few more people have jobs, but fewer jobs are being advertised
levels.body:
The government has a team that counts how many people have jobs. It is called the Office for National Statistics. It said that, between June and August, about 5 in every 100 people who wanted a job could not find one. That is a tiny bit better than a few months ago.
About 1.7 million people were looking for work. Many more adults were not looking for work at all. They may be studying, ill or looking after family.
The team said that the job market is not moving much. Fewer jobs are being advertised than before. Small firms told them that paying workers costs them more than it used to, so they are being careful about hiring.
The team will share new numbers on 17 November.
levels.why: People may find it harder to get new jobs, even though fewer are out of work.

levels.headline: Fewer jobs are being advertised, though slightly fewer people are out of work
levels.body:
The government has a team that counts jobs, called the Office for National Statistics. It says that about 5 out of every 100 people who want to work cannot find a job. That is a little better than before.
But there is a problem. Fewer jobs are being put up for people to apply for. Many small shops and firms say that paying their workers now costs them more money, so they are careful about hiring new people.
The team says the job market is not growing or shrinking much. It is staying about the same. Some people are not looking for work at all. They may be at college, unwell, or looking after a family member.
New numbers come out on 17 November.
levels.why: It can be harder to get a job when there are fewer jobs to go for.

levels.headline: Not many new jobs are on offer right now
levels.body:
Think of the jobs in the country as seats in a game of musical chairs. About 5 in every 100 grown-ups who want a seat cannot find one. That is a tiny bit better than before. But the number of new seats being offered has gone down.
The government has a team that counts all this. It says shops and small firms are being careful. They tell the team that paying workers costs them more now. So they are not asking for as many new workers.
Some grown-ups are not looking for work at all. They may be studying, feeling ill or looking after family.
The team says things are staying about the same. It will check again on 17 November.
levels.why: If there are fewer new jobs, it can take longer for grown-ups to find work.

headline: Burnham says an EU rejoin referendum in a future manifesto is 'possible', ten years on from the Brexit vote

terms.meaning: A document in which a party sets out what it promises to do if elected.
A vote in which the public decide a single question directly.
The UK's departure from the European Union, which followed the 2016 referendum.

levels.headline: Burnham says an EU rejoin referendum in a future manifesto is 'possible', ten years on from the Brexit vote
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is "possible" that a referendum on rejoining the European Union could be included in a future election manifesto, CNBC reported in early October. He made the comments to the BBC, as the country marked ten years since the 2016 Brexit referendum.
Mr Burnham became Prime Minister on 20 July, succeeding Sir Keir Starmer. A UK general election is not currently expected before 2029, so any such pledge would be for a later contest.
CNBC's coverage noted that the UK economy has largely failed to enjoy a post-Brexit boost. The remarks are a notable shift in tone on a subject that Labour leaders have often tried to avoid.
The comment is not a government policy, and no referendum has been promised.
levels.why: It shows how far the debate on Britain's relationship with Europe has moved a decade after Brexit.

levels.headline: Burnham leaves door open to a future EU referendum pledge as Brexit anniversary prompts fresh debate
levels.body:
Andy Burnham told the BBC it was "possible" a referendum on rejoining the EU could feature in a future election manifesto, according to CNBC's report from early October. The remarks came as the UK marked ten years since the 2016 vote to leave.
He has been Prime Minister since 20 July, when he succeeded Sir Keir Starmer. A general election is not currently expected before 2029, which means any commitment would be part of a later campaign rather than government policy now.
CNBC noted that the UK economy has largely failed to experience a boost since Brexit, which is part of the backdrop to the renewed discussion.
Nothing has been promised. The comment signals openness, not a plan.
levels.why: Even a hint of a rejoin vote can shape political debate and business expectations about Britain's future trade ties.

levels.headline: Burnham says a referendum on rejoining the EU is 'possible' in a future manifesto
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is "possible" that a referendum on rejoining the European Union could appear in a future election manifesto. He told the BBC this in early October, according to CNBC, just as the country marked ten years since the 2016 Brexit referendum.

This is not government policy. No referendum has been promised. His words show that the idea is not being ruled out.
levels.why: The comment shows the government is open to reopening one of the biggest political questions of the past decade.

levels.headline: Burnham says a vote on rejoining the EU is 'possible' in future

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is "possible" that a referendum on rejoining the European Union could be included in a future election manifesto. He told the BBC this in early October, as the country marked ten years since the 2016 Brexit vote, CNBC reported.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says a vote on rejoining the EU is possible in future
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is possible that a future election manifesto could promise a vote on rejoining the European Union. A manifesto is a document where a party sets out what it will do if it wins an election. This is not a promise or a plan. It only means he is not ruling the idea out.
levels.why: It shows that the argument about Britain and the EU is still alive ten years later.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says Britain could one day vote on rejoining the EU
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says a future election plan from his party could include a vote on whether Britain should rejoin the European Union. Such a plan is called a manifesto. He told the BBC it was possible. He spoke ten years after the 2016 vote, when people in Britain chose to leave the EU. That choice is known as Brexit.
He became Prime Minister in July. The next general election is not expected until 2029 at the earliest.
An American news site, CNBC, said that Britain's economy has not really grown faster since leaving the EU.
This is not a promise. He has simply said that it could happen, and that he is not ruling it out.
levels.why: It means a big question from ten years ago is being talked about again.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says Britain might vote again on rejoining the EU
levels.body:
In 2016, people in Britain voted to leave the European Union, a group of European countries that trade and work together. This was called Brexit. Now, ten years later, the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has said something interesting. He told the BBC that it is possible his party could promise a new vote on rejoining the EU at a future election.
That promise would go in a document called a manifesto, which says what a party will do if it wins.
The next election is not expected until 2029. A news site called CNBC also said that Britain's economy has not grown much faster since leaving.
There is no promise yet. He has only said it might happen.
levels.why: It shows that a decision made ten years ago is still being argued about.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says Britain could vote on joining the EU again one day
levels.body:
Ten years ago, people in Britain voted to leave the European Union. The EU is a group of European countries that work and trade together. Leaving was called Brexit. Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says it could be possible to hold another vote on joining again. He told the BBC that a party could promise this in its manifesto. A manifesto is a list of things a party says it will do if people vote for it.
He became Prime Minister in July. The next big election is not expected until 2029.
A news site said that Britain's money and business have not done much better since leaving.
He has not promised anything. He only said it could happen.
levels.why: People still disagree about whether leaving the EU was right, so this matters to many.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says there could be another vote on the EU
levels.body:
Ten years ago, the people of Britain voted to leave a club of European countries called the European Union. The countries in the club trade and work together. Now the Prime Minister, who is called Andy Burnham, has said there could be another vote about joining again one day. A vote like this, where everyone gets to choose, is called a referendum.
He said a party might say so in its manifesto. A manifesto is a list of promises before an election. The next big election is not until 2029 or later.
He has not promised anything. He just said it could be possible. People who like the idea and people who do not will both be listening.
levels.why: Many people feel strongly about this, and it could change how Britain trades with Europe.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister says there might one day be another big vote
levels.body:
Imagine your class once voted to leave a big after-school club. Ten years later, some people wonder if it was a good idea. They ask whether you should vote again to rejoin. Something like this is happening in Britain. Ten years ago, people voted to leave a group of European countries called the European Union.
Now the Prime Minister, who is called Andy Burnham, has said there could be another vote one day. He has not promised it. He has only said it is possible.
The next big election is not until 2029 at the earliest, so nothing will happen soon.
Some people would love another vote, and some people would hate the idea.
levels.why: Big choices like this can change how we trade, travel and work with our neighbours.

headline: Government orders independent review of security for people in public life after Widdecombe killing

terms.meaning: The police network that investigates terrorism offences.

The committee that decides what protection public figures receive.

levels.headline: Government orders independent review of security for people in public life after Widdecombe killing
levels.body:
The Home Secretary has announced an independent, root-and-branch review of the protective security the state provides to people in public life, GOV.UK says. It will be led by Sir Stephen Lovegrove, the former national security adviser, and is due to report within six months.
The review follows the killing of the former MP Ann Widdecombe. Police described it as a targeted attack, and Counter Terrorism Policing took over the case after new evidence emerged. The suspect has been charged with murder and also with a terrorism offence, including preparing an act of terror against the leader of Reform UK. The charges are allegations, and the case is for the courts.
The government also offered the Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, a meeting with the chair of RAVEC, the body that manages protection for public figures, and announced sanctions on two individuals linked to Iranian espionage.
levels.why: It could change how politicians and other public figures are protected from threats.

levels.headline: Independent security review launched as terrorism charge follows Widdecombe killing

The Home Secretary has ordered a full, independent review of how the state protects people in public life, such as politicians. Sir Stephen Lovegrove, who used to be the government's national security adviser, will lead it. He has six months to report.

levels.why: Politicians need to be safe to do their jobs, and voters need to be able to speak to them.

levels.headline: A new review will look at how politicians and other public figures are kept safe

The Home Secretary has asked for a big, independent review of how the state keeps people in public life safe. Sir Stephen Lovegrove, who was the country's top national security adviser, will run it. He has six months to finish.

levels.why: It is about keeping public figures safe so that they can do their jobs.

levels.headline: The government wants a full check on how public figures are kept safe

levels.why: People in politics need to be safe, so that they can speak freely and do their work.

levels.headline: The government is checking how well politicians are kept safe
levels.body:
A former MP called Ann Widdecombe was killed. Police say the attack was on purpose. A man has been charged with murder. He has also been charged with a terrorism crime, which includes planning an attack on the leader of the Reform UK party. These are only charges. A court has to decide if they are true.

levels.why: It is meant to make sure people who work in politics are protected.

levels.headline: Leaders will check how politicians are kept safe
levels.body:
A former MP, called Ann Widdecombe, was killed. This is very sad. Police say someone attacked on purpose. A man has been charged, but a court will decide if he did it.
Because of this, a minister called the Home Secretary has asked for a big check of how the people who work in politics are kept safe. A man called Sir Stephen Lovegrove, who used to give security advice to the government, will lead it. He has six months to finish his work.
The government has also offered to talk to Nigel Farage, who leads a political party, about keeping that person safe.
The aim is to make sure people can do their jobs safely.
levels.why: People who work for us should be safe when they do their jobs.

levels.headline: Grown-ups are checking that people who lead us are kept safe
levels.body:
Some people have jobs where they speak up for us and make big choices. They are called politicians. Sadly, one former politician called Ann Widdecombe was killed. The police say someone attacked on purpose. A man has been charged, and a court will decide what happened.
A government minister called the Home Secretary wants to make sure other politicians are safe. So the Home Secretary has asked a careful grown-up, called Sir Stephen Lovegrove, to look at how well they are protected. It is a bit like a teacher checking that every door in school has a good lock. He has six months to finish.
The government has also offered to talk to Nigel Farage about their safety.
levels.why: Leaders must be safe so that they can do their jobs for everybody.

headline: Student List wins Serbian election as Vučić concedes defeat, ending 14 years of rule

The process of a country joining the European Union.

levels.headline: Student List wins Serbian election as Vučić concedes defeat, ending 14 years of rule
levels.body:
Serbian leader Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat in Sunday's snap parliamentary election on 25 October, telling supporters at his party's election night event that "The Students' List has won". The result ends his 14 years in power, according to Euronews and CNBC.
Vučić projected that the Student List would take between 135 and 140 of parliament's 250 seats, with his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) on around 105. He said SNS won about 1.7 million votes against about 2.2 million for the students. Final results had not been confirmed, and reports differ on seat details.
The Student List is the electoral arm of a student-led movement that grew out of a deadly disaster at a recently renovated railway station in November 2024. Vučić resigned on 27 September to run for prime minister.
EU leaders, including Costa and von der Leyen, welcomed the result.
levels.why: A change of government in Serbia could reshape its relations with the EU and Russia, and its democracy.

levels.headline: Serbia's students win election in 'political earthquake' as Vučić admits defeat
levels.body:
Aleksandar Vučić admitted defeat in Serbia's snap parliamentary election on 25 October, saying: "The Students' List has won." The result ends his 14-year rule, Euronews reported.
By his own projection the Student List will win 135 to 140 of the 250 seats and his SNS party about 105. He said SNS took around 1.7 million votes against around 2.2 million for the students. levels.headline: Lula wins Brazil's presidential runoff 51.8% to 48.2% but Bolsonaro refuses to concede
levels.body:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won Brazil's presidential runoff on 25 October with 51.8% of the vote to 48.2% for Flávio Bolsonaro, a margin of roughly 4.4 million votes, according to the Superior Electoral Court. Lula had trailed in the first round, and no candidate in that position had won the second round since 1989.
Bolsonaro has not conceded. He says he does not recognise the result and will challenge it in court, pointing to a late Supreme Court order that extended voting by two hours. Euronews also reported that Donald Trump said, without evidence, that the election looked "rigged".
Lula's allies did poorly in Congress. Bolsonaro's Liberal Party will hold 121 of 513 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 28 of 81 in the Senate from February 2027, against 88 for Lula's Workers' Party federation, which will make his reforms hard to pass.
levels.why: The result ends a run of conservative wins in Latin America, but Lula faces a hostile Congress and a disputed outcome.

Bolsonaro refuses to concede and says he will go to court, citing a last-minute Supreme Court order that extended voting by two hours. Trump said, without evidence, that the election looked "rigged", Euronews reported.

Brazil-linked stocks fell on Monday.
levels.why: A disputed result and a right-leaning Congress could make Brazil harder to govern.

levels.headline: Brent crude closes at $115.81 as Saudi and Qatari diplomacy over the US-Iran war keeps oil near wartime highs
levels.body:
Brent crude futures closed at $115.81 a barrel on Monday 26 October, down 91 cents, after briefly topping $117 earlier in the session, CNBC reported. In early trading Euronews said Brent had fallen more than 6%, retreating from its highest close since March, as regional mediators headed to Tehran. Most of that drop was reversed by the close.
Saudi Arabia's defence minister met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Tehran to try to de-escalate the war between the US and Iran. Qatari mediators were also reported to have travelled to Tehran in coordination with Washington. On Tuesday, December Brent slipped 0.87% to $114.80 as hopes of de-escalation grew, though CNBC noted losses were limited.
Kpler data show Gulf crude exports, excluding Iran, returned to pre-war levels in September, though more now bypasses the Strait of Hormuz via pipelines.
levels.why: Oil prices feed straight into petrol, heating and inflation, so diplomacy in Tehran matters far beyond the region.

headline: Israel votes in a wartime election seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, with neither bloc polling a majority

levels.headline: Israel votes in a wartime election seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, with neither bloc polling a majority
levels.body:
Israel holds its general election today, Tuesday 27 October, the last date allowed by law. Euronews and CNBC describe it as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership since the Gaza war began in 2023.
Recent polls show neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the main opposition bloc reaching the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. That leaves smaller parties and Arab parties potentially pivotal in forming a coalition. The main opposition challenger is the centrist former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.
The campaign has centred on Netanyahu himself: his character, his responsibility for the security failures of 7 October, military exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men and his 2023 attempt to overhaul the judiciary. It also takes place against the war with Iran and Hamas.
Results were not available when this edition was written.
levels.why: The result will shape Israel's wartime policy and the wider search for peace in the Middle East.

levels.headline: Israel has a big vote today
levels.body:
Today, grown-ups in Israel are voting to choose their leaders. Israel is a country in the Middle East. It has been in a long war since 2023, so this vote is a big deal. The leaders they choose will have to decide what to do about it.
Many people see the vote as a test of the Prime Minister, who is called Benjamin Netanyahu. Some people want Netanyahu to stay. Others want a change. His main rival is a man called Gadi Eisenkot, who used to lead the army.
Before the vote, the polls said that nobody would win more than half the seats. So smaller parties may need to join up with bigger ones.
We do not know who won yet.
levels.why: The leaders chosen will decide about a war that affects many people.

levels.headline: A country is choosing its leaders today
levels.body:
Imagine your school has to choose a new head pupil. Two groups both want the job. Each group has lots of friends. But neither group has more than half of the votes. So they must ask the smaller groups to join them. That could be how things go in Israel today.
Israel is a country in the Middle East. Grown-ups there are voting to choose their leaders. The leader in charge now is called Benjamin Netanyahu. His main rival is called Gadi Eisenkot.
Israel has been in a long war since 2023, so many people care a lot about this vote.
We do not know who won yet. We will find out soon.
levels.why: Leaders make big choices, so people pay close attention to who wins.

headline: Eurozone growth slows to a four-month low as France slips into contraction, ahead of the ECB's 29 October meeting

terms.meaning: Purchasing Managers' Index, a monthly survey of firms where a reading above 50 means growth and below 50 means shrinking.
A figure combining the results for manufacturing and services.
The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the countries that use the euro.

levels.headline: Eurozone growth slows to a four-month low as France slips into contraction, ahead of the ECB's 29 October meeting
levels.body:
The eurozone's composite Purchasing Managers' Index fell to 51.9 in October from 53.1 in September, its weakest reading in four months, though still above the 50 mark that separates growth from contraction, Euronews reported.
France was the main drag. Its composite PMI dropped to 48.4 from 51.1, well below the 50.5 economists had expected, with firms citing weaker demand and continued job cuts. Oxford Economics blamed political uncertainty and higher government borrowing costs. Germany's index eased to 52.8 from 53.8, against a forecast of 53.3.
S&P Global's Chris Williamson still sees quarterly GDP growth of around 0.3% in the survey data but warned that higher interest rates are starting to take a toll. Eurozone inflation hit 3.8% in September, a three-year high, according to CNBC.
The European Central Bank is widely expected to hold rates when it meets on 29 October.
levels.why: Weaker growth with high inflation puts the ECB in a difficult spot, and it affects UK exports to Europe.

levels.headline: France falls into contraction as eurozone activity cools, with high inflation complicating the ECB's task
levels.body:
Euronews reported that the eurozone composite PMI slipped to 51.9 in October from 53.1, a four-month low but still in growth territory above 50.
France dragged on the bloc, with its composite index falling to 48.4 from 51.1, far below the 50.5 forecast. Companies reported weaker demand and more job cuts, and Oxford Economics attributed it to political volatility and higher government borrowing costs. Germany's index eased to 52.8 from 53.8.
S&P Global's Chris Williamson still sees GDP growth of about 0.3% a quarter in the survey data, but said higher interest rates are beginning to dampen demand. Meanwhile, eurozone inflation reached 3.8% in September, the highest in three years, CNBC reported.
The ECB is widely expected to leave rates unchanged at its meeting on 29 October.
levels.why: Falling activity alongside high inflation is the awkward mix that stretches central banks.

levels.headline: Eurozone business growth slows and French firms report shrinking activity
levels.body:
A survey of businesses in the eurozone shows growth is slowing. The composite Purchasing Managers' Index, a monthly gauge of business activity, fell to 51.9 in October from 53.1 in September. That is its lowest in four months, though any reading above 50 still means growth.
France was the weakest. Its index fell to 48.4 from 51.1, below 50 and well under the 50.5 economists expected. Firms reported weaker demand and kept cutting jobs. Oxford Economics blamed political uncertainty and higher government borrowing costs. Germany's reading eased to 52.8.
S&P Global's Chris Williamson said higher interest rates are starting to reduce demand. Eurozone inflation was 3.8% in September, a three-year high.
The European Central Bank is expected to hold rates on 29 October.
levels.why: Slower growth in Europe can hurt British exporters and keeps pressure on interest rates.

levels.headline: Eurozone growth slows to a four-month low as France contracts
levels.body:
Business activity across the eurozone is growing more slowly. The composite Purchasing Managers' Index fell to 51.9 in October from 53.1 in September, the weakest in four months, though still above the 50 line that separates growth from shrinking.
France was the weak spot. Its index dropped to 48.4 from 51.1, well below the 50.5 forecast, with companies reporting lower demand and continued job cuts. Oxford Economics blamed political uncertainty and higher government borrowing costs. Germany's index eased to 52.8.
Prices are also rising fast, with eurozone inflation at 3.8% in September, a three-year high. S&P Global's Chris Williamson warned that higher interest rates are starting to dampen demand.
The European Central Bank is expected to hold rates when it meets on 29 October.
levels.why: Slow growth combined with high inflation makes life harder for businesses, workers and central banks.

levels.headline: Europe's economy is slowing, and France's businesses are now shrinking
levels.body:
A monthly survey of businesses across the countries that use the euro shows their growth is slowing. The survey gives a score, where 50 means no change and anything above means growth. The eurozone score fell to 51.9 in October from 53.1 in September. That is the lowest in four months, but it is still above 50.
France did worst. Its score fell to 48.4, which means business there is shrinking. Companies said customers were buying less, and they kept cutting jobs. Experts say political uncertainty and higher costs for the government to borrow are partly to blame. Germany's score eased to 52.8.
Prices are also rising quickly, by 3.8% in September. The European Central Bank is expected to leave interest rates alone on 29 October.
levels.why: Slow growth and high prices at the same time make life harder for businesses and families.

levels.headline: Business growth in Europe is slowing down, and France's economy is shrinking
levels.body:
Every month, people ask businesses across Europe how busy they are. The answers become a score. A score of 50 means nothing is changing. A score above 50 means businesses are growing. In October the score for the countries that use the euro fell to 51.9, from 53.1 the month before. That is the lowest in four months, but it still shows some growth.
France is doing worse. Its score fell to 48.4, which means its businesses are shrinking. Firms there said that customers were buying less and they were cutting jobs. Germany's score fell a bit, to 52.8.
Prices are going up fast in Europe, by 3.8% in September. The bank that looks after the euro is expected to keep interest rates the same on 29 October.
levels.why: If business slows and prices rise, jobs and shopping budgets can both feel the strain.

levels.headline: Europe's businesses are growing more slowly, and French ones are shrinking
levels.body:
Each month, people ask businesses in Europe how busy they have been. The answers turn into a score. If the score is 50, nothing has changed. If it is above 50, businesses are growing. In October, the score for the countries that use the euro, a type of money, fell to 51.9. A month earlier it was 53.1. It is the lowest in four months, but it is still growing a little.
France did worse. Its score fell to 48.4, so its businesses are shrinking. They said fewer customers were buying, and they were letting workers go. Germany's score dipped too.
Prices are going up by 3.8% a year. The bank that looks after the euro is likely to leave its interest rate alone on 29 October.
levels.why: Slow business and rising prices can make life harder for workers and shoppers.

levels.headline: Businesses in Europe are not doing as well as before, especially in France
levels.body:
Each month, people ask businesses in Europe how busy they are. They turn the answers into a score. A score of 50 means nothing has changed. If it is higher than 50, businesses are growing. If it is lower, they are shrinking. In October, the score for the countries that use the euro, a type of money, was 51.9. That is lower than last month, when it was 53.1.
France's score was only 48.4. So its businesses are getting smaller. They said fewer people were buying, and they let some workers go. Germany's score went down a little too.
Prices have also been going up by 3.8% a year. The bank that looks after the euro is expected to leave interest rates alone on 29 October.
levels.why: If businesses do worse, some people may lose work or find fewer jobs.

levels.headline: Shops and firms in Europe are selling a bit less
levels.body:
Each month, people ask shops and firms in Europe how busy they have been. They turn the answers into a score. If the score is higher than 50, businesses are growing. If it is lower than 50, they are shrinking. In October, the score for the countries that use the euro was 51.9. That is still growing, but more slowly than before.
In France, the score was 48.4. That means French firms were selling less. They said fewer customers were buying, and some firms let workers go.
Prices are also going up quite fast across Europe. The bank that looks after the euro, a type of money, will meet on 29 October. People think it will leave its interest rate the same.
levels.why: When businesses sell less, workers can lose jobs and families can have less money to spend.

levels.headline: Some shops and firms in Europe are doing a little worse
levels.body:
Imagine a school fair with stalls selling cakes and drinks. Last month the stalls were busy and sold a lot. This month, they are still selling but not quite as much. That is a little like what is happening in Europe.
Every month, people ask businesses in Europe how busy they have been. In October, the answer was that they were still doing OK, but not as well as before. In one country, France, the answer was worse. French businesses are selling less and some are letting workers go.
Things in shops are also getting dearer. The bank that looks after the euro, a type of money, will meet on 29 October. People think it will leave its rates the same.
levels.why: When firms sell less, workers can worry about their jobs.

headline: Anthropic files publicly for a Nasdaq listing, with seven founders set to hold 50.1% of voting power

terms.meaning: Initial public offering, when a company first sells its shares to the public on a stock exchange.
The registration document a company files with the US regulator, the SEC, before going public.
The power to decide company matters such as who sits on the board.

levels.headline: Anthropic files publicly for a Nasdaq listing, with seven founders set to hold 50.1% of voting power
levels.body:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, has publicly filed its S-1 registration with the US Securities and Exchange Commission and plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT", CNBC reported on 26 October. It had filed confidentially in June.
The filing says seven co-founders will hold 50.1% of the voting power through a new entity called Founder LLC. The Long-Term Benefit Trust, which elects and removes most of the board, remains in place.
Press reports on the filing say it devotes many pages to risks from artificial intelligence, including a warning of catastrophic or existential risk, and flags customer concentration, with nearly a quarter of 2025 revenue from two clients. Some details come from Reuters and have not been checked against the document itself.
CNBC did not report a pricing date. The news lifted AI-linked shares on Monday.
levels.why: A listing of this scale would test investor appetite for AI and show how a safety-focused company handles public ownership.

levels.headline: Anthropic goes public with its IPO filing as founders keep 50.1% of the votes
levels.body:
Anthropic has publicly filed an S-1 registration with the SEC and intends to list on the Nasdaq with the ticker "ANT", according to CNBC on 26 October. The company first filed confidentially in June.
The document sets out governance in which seven co-founders hold 50.1% of the voting power through a new entity called Founder LLC, while the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which elects and removes most of the board, continues.
Reports on the prospectus say that a large share of its pages cover AI risks, including a warning of catastrophic or existential risk to humanity, and that nearly a quarter of 2025 revenue came from two customers. Some figures are from Reuters, citing a leaked copy.
No pricing date has been confirmed. The filing helped lift technology shares on Monday.
levels.why: The filing shows how AI companies balance fast growth with public warnings about risk and tight founder control.

levels.headline: Anthropic files to float on the Nasdaq, with founders keeping control
levels.body:
Anthropic, which makes the AI assistant Claude, has made its stock market filing public. It is called an S-1 and was sent to the US regulator, the SEC. The company plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT". It had filed in private in June, CNBC reported on 26 October.
Under the plan, seven co-founders will hold 50.1% of the voting power through a new company called Founder LLC. A body called the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which chooses most of the board, stays.
Reports say the document spends many pages on the risks of artificial intelligence, including a warning of existential risk, and that nearly a quarter of 2025 revenue came from two clients. Some of these details come from Reuters and are not confirmed.
No date has been set for the share sale.
levels.why: It could be one of the largest stock market debuts for an AI company.

levels.headline: Anthropic makes its stock market filing public and plans a Nasdaq listing

The filing says seven co-founders will hold 50.1% of the voting power through a new entity called Founder LLC, while the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which elects and removes most of the board, stays in place.
